Les mesures de contrôle des armes à feu: Can gun control measures make the public safer?
La culture des armes à feu témoigne de l: Gun culture reflects the transformation that has taken place in the industry.
Cet été, de nombreuses fusillades ont eu: This summer, there were numerous shootings in neighbourhoods in Montréal, in Laval and in the surrounding areas. Shots fired in broad daylight and stray bullets are shattering residents’ sense of peace. For a few hundred dollars and without a licence, young people can get their hands on guns quickly and easily. How do the guns end up in their hands?
Dans la majorité des cas, ce sont des ar: In most cases, these are illegal guns that organized crime brings across the Canada-U.S. border. “With one of the longest unfortified borders in the world, there are holes everywhere where trafficking is possible,” explains Paul Laurier, a retired Sûreté du Québec investigator. “Guns are very easy to find, far too easy, and selling them is lucrative,” says the former investigator, who worked on organized crime and terrorism. “If Quebec police took away every firearm, I guarantee you that within a month the guns would be back.”
Il lie cette éventualité à la proximité: He links this possibility to the proximity of the U.S. market and to the channels between the two countries run by organized crime. According to Francis Langlois, a researcher specializing in firearms in Canada and the United States at the Raoul-Dandurand Chair, the American market is too big and American gun laws are weak. “It’s extremely difficult to counter, and the supply in the United States is practically unlimited. But that’s really where the guns are found. The problem is our neighbour,” he says. However, the specialist believes that controlling the border will change nothing about violence in big cities if there is no upstream investment in violence prevention. Former investigator Paul Laurier agrees.
« Ce n'est pas la réglementation des arm: “It’s not gun regulation that’s going to fix the problem. It takes people who go out and talk to the youth and break the cycle,” he says. “If we transform the socio-economic conditions in the neighbourhoods most affected by this violence, young people will be able to find a different path.” “Guns make this violence deadlier, more dangerous. They don’t necessarily raise crime rates, but they multiply the chances of being killed,” adds Francis Langlois.
La culture des armes à feu témoigne de l: Gun culture reflects the transformation that has taken place in the industry. “Starting in the 1980s, we ended up with military-style and police-style weapons, semi-automatic weapons,” says Francis Langlois. These weapons weren’t on the market before.
« Il y également la diffusion de l’image: “There is also the spread of the image of the gun as a way to assert your masculinity, to protect yourself. It’s a narrative perpetuated by the industry, and that narrative creates a more aggressive gun culture,” says the researcher. The market now offers semi-automatic pistols that can hold 10, 15 or 20 rounds. Assault rifles can hold up to 100 rounds.

Langlois indique que la tuerie de la: Mr. Langlois says the Polytechnique massacre would not have been possible without a weapon that could hold 30 rounds. “There’s a whole discipline of rapid-fire shooting, and it’s new. It developed in the 1990s and 2000s. They’re selling not just guns, but an entire culture.”
« Dans les rues, les tueries, ça ne se p: “On the streets, the killings aren’t happening with long guns. Yes, those cause damage too, but the danger is handguns,” says Paul Laurier. Echoing the former investigator, researcher Francis Langlois also argues that the illegal handguns that end up in the hands of street gangs come from the United States. The specialist says he doesn’t understand the emphasis on handgun control in the public debate, since most of those guns come from illegal arms trafficking. In his view, then, legal controls won’t solve the underlying problem. Some of the handguns found on the street are nonetheless domestic: they are stolen from the legal market or sold to unlicensed individuals by licensed owners. Nathalie Provost, spokesperson for the organization PolySeSouvient, tells us that the number of handguns held by legal owners has doubled in the past ten years.
D’après Statistique Canada, on compte ma: According to Statistics Canada, there are now nearly a million handguns on the legal market. Several federal parties have weighed in on handgun control, relegating it to municipalities or provinces. Francis Langlois and Nathalie Provost both believe that national control is necessary and that such measures are not effective without it.
« Même si on interdit des armes légales: “Even if you ban legal guns within the city of Montréal, that doesn’t stop guns from coming into and going out of cities,” says Mr. Langlois. He cites the gunman in the 2018 shooting on Danforth Avenue in Toronto, who obtained his handgun illegally in Toronto. The gun in question had been sold legally in Saskatchewan.
« Quand on réglemente les armes légales,: “When we regulate legal guns, it’s mainly to limit mass shootings,” says the researcher. In his view, the goal of controlling military-style weapons such as assault weapons, which have enormous firepower, is tied to public safety in terms of suicides, accidental use and mass shootings. Most of the guns used in this type of mass tragedy were purchased legally, notably the weapons used at the Quebec City mosque and at Dawson College.
« Ce sont armes qui sont prisées par des: “These are weapons prized by mass killers. That’s why governments and organizations are looking to tighten gun control. They are ideal weapons for soldiers or police officers, but they aren’t made to be used by civilians,” he says.
Depuis la destruction du registre canadi: Since the Harper government destroyed the Canadian firearms registry in 2012, Canada has had no precise data on the number of non-restricted firearms (hunting rifles and long guns) in circulation in the country. It is therefore very difficult to know how many guns a non-restricted firearms licence holder owns. The Canadian government has thus lost track of many of the hunting rifles and assault weapons that were purchased. While the mandatory buyback program proposed by the Liberal Party is, in principle, interesting, it will be difficult to enforce, the researcher says. Charles, a non-restricted firearms licence holder who does sport shooting, bears this out. He owns 11 firearms, including 3 assault weapons.
Aucune de ses armes est sur le décret de: None of his guns is covered by the 2020 order in council. The young man has several friends who also own legal firearms. He says the mandatory buyback program mentioned in the May 2020 order has become a running gag in the firearms community.
«Si on ne sait pas combien de personnes: “If we don’t know how many people own this type of weapon, there’s an obvious loophole. Who’s going to tell the government they have one?” he asks. “What the order does is end the trade in these weapons in Canada. So there’s no longer any avenue for legitimate use of them, since we no longer have the right to transport, trade, own or use them.
Ce n’est pas pas parfait, mais si l’on v: It’s not perfect, but if you want to get these weapons off the market, it’s a good measure,” the specialist explains. Without a registry of non-restricted firearms, it is hard to legislate, explains Francis Langlois. “It was the best thing we had, it was destroyed and it isn’t coming back. It cost too much,” says Nathalie Provost of the firearms registry. The PolySeSouvient spokesperson believes no party goes far enough in controlling assault weapons, for fear of losing votes if they propose measures that are too strict on legal firearms.
PolySeSouvient s’indigne de l’argument d: PolySeSouvient is outraged by the Conservatives’ argument that they <l1>don’t want to “blame” gun owners who follow the rules</l1> with too many restrictions on legal firearms. “It gives the impression that Trudeau is harassing honest owners, when all he wants is to remove overly powerful guns. We have nothing against the good owners, we’re not taking away their ability to shoot, we’re taking away certain models,” says the Polytechnique massacre survivor.
Elle s’indigne du fait que la puissance: She is outraged that a citizen’s firepower can be greater than a police officer’s. Ms. Provost believes the government should ban all assault weapons, and that they have no place in the hands of citizens.
« Dans tous les pays, où il y a un contr: “In every country with tighter gun control, there are fewer deaths linked to guns. I’m not saying it will solve the whole problem of illegal guns, we’re not naive,” she says. She draws a comparison with vehicles. “Do you realize that a firearm is less controlled than a car? Cars are registered, and all our governments know who owns how many cars. That’s not the case with firearms,” she says. The registry gave law enforcement the information it needed to act.
<strong>Un permis trop facile à obtenir?: A licence that’s too easy to get?
« Ce n’est pas difficile d’avoir un perm: “It’s not hard to get a firearms licence, but it’s very bureaucratic,” explains Charles, who got his licence in six months. After taking a <l1>Canadian Firearms Safety Course</l1>, he wrote the exam the same day. “Basically, you just can’t point the gun at the instructor and you have to show minimal competence in handling firearms,” he says mockingly. A few weeks later, he received his certificate and could fill out a firearms possession licence application on the RCMP website. After a few months, Charles received a non-restricted firearms licence, allowing him to buy long guns and hunting rifles. No psychological evaluation, no need to justify why he is applying for a firearms licence. “No need to say it’s for sport,” he says.
« Il y a des questions sur antécédents c: “There are questions about criminal and violent history, but there’s no question on the form about extremist ideologies, and for mental health, it’s self-declared,” the young man notes. The form asks for two references who vouch for the applicant’s ability to obtain a possession and acquisition licence “in the interest of the safety of the applicant or of any other person.” Charles would like more steps to be taken to make sure that people who want a firearms licence are of sound mind. He believes the debate doesn’t address this aspect enough. “You can always make the licence harder to get, but you have to invest the resources to actually do the checks,” agrees researcher Francis Langlois.
